tracking.$description: How far the letters sit from each other. A theme has a real opinion here — the open end is what separates a plain label from a shouted one — so the ramp is tokens rather than the handful of `em` values the utilities would otherwise carry.

leading.$description: How far the lines sit from each other. A theme has a real opinion here — the open end is what separates a poster from a wall of text — so the ramp is tokens rather than the handful of bare numbers the utilities would otherwise carry.

brand.$description: Brand — the lockup wordmark voice spending font.family.brand.

spacing.$description: The spacing scale. Every gap, pad and inset is one of these steps.

radius.$description: Corner rounding, from square to fully round.

border.$description: Stroke weight. Every control and surface reads `width`, so a theme changes its edge weight in one place; the numbered steps above it are the ladder a layout reaches for when one edge needs to say more than the rest.

width.$description: The hairline every control and surface draws with.

width-2.$description: The emphasis edge: a control that must read as selected rather than merely bordered.

width-4.$description: The heavy edge. Rare on purpose — a stroke this thick is a statement, not a divider.

width-8.$description: The frame. A block drawn rather than outlined.

style.$description: Named border tuples: the width, style and ink of an edge in one token. A rule spreads the tuple; a theme restates one field to move every border built from it.

0.$description: Gone, not merely faint. The step a rule reaches for when the element should not be painted at all.

5.$description: Barely there: a wash of colour behind content that must stay fully legible.

10.$description: A ghost: present in the DOM, gone from the eye. Reserved for decoration.

15.$description: A whisper above the ghost step: decoration that must survive a bright room.

20.$description: Disabled. Low enough to stop a control being pressed, high enough to keep its label readable beside live controls.

25.$description: A quarter: the step between disabled and dimmed, for scrims that must not flatten what they cover.

30.$description: A disabled control on a dark surface, where the same fraction reads lighter than it does on a light one.

35.$description: Between dimmed and half: a track filling, a hint gaining weight.

40.$description: The dimmed step: a placeholder image, a track before it is filled, a hint of content.

45.$description: Just under half: content that yields without disappearing.

50.$description: Half. The step most rules ask for, so it is the one a theme is most likely to have an opinion about.

55.$description: Just over half: content that asserts itself without taking over.

60.$description: Muted but still read: text on a disabled field that the reader is expected to transcribe.

65.$description: Between muted and secondary: emphasis that has not yet arrived.

70.$description: Secondary content that must survive a projector or a bright room.

75.$description: Three quarters: a scrim that dims without hiding, a wash that tints without covering.

80.$description: A hair under full strength: the hover state of something that should feel nearly solid.

85.$description: Almost there: an overlay the reader looks through without noticing.

90.$description: Almost opaque. The step for a scrim that must dim what is behind it without appearing to.

95.$description: A breath under full: a veil that reads as solid until it moves.

100.$description: Fully shown. The default, named so a rule can say it rather than assume it.

opacity.$description: How much of a thing is shown, as a fraction. A theme owns this because the same fraction reads differently over a light surface than over a dark one, and because `disabled` is a decision about how present a dead control still looks.

motion.$description: How things move and how long it takes.

loop.$description: The period of an endless animation: the skeleton's pulse and the loop utilities. A loop is watched rather than reacted to, so it is slower than any transition — and never faster than the floor below which it reads as a strobe.

breakpoint.$description: Viewport widths where layout steps change.

z-index.$description: Stacking order. Layer, never a magic number at the call site.

icon.$description: Glyph sizes, from the reader's own root rather than the element they sit in — a step has to be a jump, and an `em` step against 14px prose is 2px.

avatar.$description: How big an avatar is, as the edge of the square it fills. A theme owns the ladder because the size of a face is a design decision, not a product of some other token.

sm.$description: The size for a face in a list or a comment: it reads beside its label without leading the row.

md.$description: The default: a face beside a name, or a profile header at rest.

lg.$description: A face as the subject of a page: a profile header at the top of a long column.

focus.$description: The focus ring, shared by every interactive element: buttons, links, fields, summaries and dialogs.

width.$description: The ring's stroke. Two pixels in both modes: a one-pixel ring reads as a rendering artifact rather than a decision.
